Bah, late to the thread, but I'll pitch in an idea anyway -

Earth and Beyond succeeds, EVE Online fails.

Setting aside what it'd mean to have a world without EVE (a great game, but not one that to my eye has inspired any real change in the industry), the success of Earth and Beyond could've saved Westwood studios from oblivion.

Subsequent C&C titles (Tiberian/Red Alert/Generals) are no longer hackneyed EA bullshit, but are instead still guided by the original creators at Westwood. Instead of - for the most part - fading into relative obscurity and irrelevance, the RTS genre enjoys a period of flourishing as a series of successes by Westwood keep it in the public eye. Starcraft 2 releases years earlier to take advantage of this trend. The competitive games scene continues to be dominated by RTS games. MOBAs exist, thanks to Warcraft 3 modders (DotA being the original), but never achieve the level of competitive popularity that they enjoy in our reality and fewer DotA clones exist (maybe we get, e.g., League of Legends, but no Smite or Heroes of the Storm).

The protagonist's method might be essentially a health bar displayed as hearts, but their chosen method of expanding that health bar - namely, finding 'pieces of heart' in the world, as well as heart containers off of bosses - has made it one of the most iconic health systems in the industry. By linking your health bar not only to progress but *crucially* also to exploration, the designers incentivized a style of play (exploration, risk-taking, careful examination of all environments) that the game might otherwise not have encouraged.

The original platformer games where your health was 'I'm big!' or 'I'm small!' was fairly unique, and I'm not sure anything else has ever really approached it. Sort of a shame that the new entries in that franchise have abandoned it. No, '1 hit and you're dead, or 2 hits with this powerup' is not in and of itself unique, but the changing size of your character actually had a tangible effect on how you could control your avatar, secret areas you could reach, powerups available (no fire flowers if you're small!), etc.

I've always appreciated the fighting game series' approach to health as well, counting up instead of down. Most, if not all, fighting games have mechanics that allow a talented player to survive a long time even at low health - dodging, blocking, whatever. And these games have these as well, but there's an added layer in the health system. Doesn't matter if somebody punts you up to 400% damage, so long as you avoid getting hit it is just a number.

Finally, though it tragically kicked off the 'regenerating health bars' craze, the original first-person shooter's regenerating shields system was very well implemented, and combined with the sound cues used when shields were depleted and regenerating allowed you to focus on the fight instead of your health and shields, listening for how your health was doing instead of pulling your eyes away from your targets to look.
